title: Champions vs native Ascend aclnn (CANN 9.0.0), measured 2026-11-07

protocol.pypto_side: frozen remote_harness.py (sha256 5c7b7aa4... identical across all domain verifiers and /root/ptocontri/pkg), latency_us = median per-round effective_us (PYPTO_BENCH=1)
protocol.aclnn_side: tools/aclnn_bench.py (pyacl + ctypes on libopapi.so): wall-clock per round (enqueue aclnn call(s) + acl.rt.synchronize_stream), median; aclnn executor fetched once via *GetWorkspaceSize, marked repeatable, reused across rounds. Both sides are end-to-end wall clock including host dispatch.
protocol.shape_policy: m-tier decision preset {M:4096, N:4096}; dtype = champion's native contract dtype (bf16)

aclnn_baseline_semantics: Two native baselines. (1) aclnnAddRmsNorm(x, res, gamma, epsilon=1e-6, y, rstd, xOut=h) — the native FUSED op, same semantics as our kernel (outputs y, rstd and the sum h). Constraint found on-machine: aclnn requires gamma as 1-D [N] in the input dtype (bf16); our contract keeps gamma fp32 and multiplies in fp32, so the native path rounds gamma to bf16 first (verified correct within bf16 tolerance). (2) aclnnAdd + aclnnRmsNorm — the unfused decomposition a user writes without a fused kernel; note its norm input is the bf16-rounded sum, unlike our kernel which norms the fp32 sum.

aclnn_alternative.note: the unfused aclnn decomposition is FASTER than the native fused aclnnAddRmsNorm at this shape (100.05 vs 121.47 us); our champion beats both.

convention: speedup_pypto_vs_aclnn = aclnn_us / pypto_us; >1 means the pypto champion is faster
